landing.heroDescription: Kivvi is the ERP for businesses giving goods a second life: thrift stores, IT refurbishers, repair cafés, vintage shops. Per-item tracking, AI quick entry, Swiss QR invoices — all in one system.
landing.originStory: Kivvi was built at revamp-it — one of Switzerland's largest IT refurbishers. Since 2003 they take in electronics, test, repair, and resell them. After years with ERPs that were never designed for secondhand, they built their own. Now it's open source — for all circular economy businesses.

hero.title: Frequently asked questions
hero.subtitle: Everything you want to know before getting started.

questions.a: Kivvi is an open-source ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) built specifically for circular-economy businesses — thrift stores, IT refurbishers, repair cafés, vintage shops, and similar organisations. It manages the full lifecycle of goods: from intake through condition grading and repair to sale and impact measurement. Kivvi is built in Switzerland and natively supports Swiss law (QR invoicing, VAT, donation rules).

Yes. Kivvi is released under the MIT license — you can use, host, modify, and redistribute it for free. There are no license fees, no subscription fees, no freemium model. The only costs are infrastructure (server, backup) when you self-host — or any external hosting service you choose.

Yes, Kivvi is designed for self-hosting. You need a server with PostgreSQL and Node.js. Setup takes about an hour for technically capable people. Your data stays fully under your control — no cloud provider has access. For businesses without their own IT we offer hosted instances.

Kivvi is built for businesses giving goods a second life: thrift stores and social department stores, IT refurbishers and computer recyclers, repair cafés and workshops, vintage shops and clothing exchanges, bike refurbishers, upcycling ateliers, and non-profits with goods logistics. Anyone selling new goods is better served by a standard ERP.

The interface is available in German (Switzerland), English, and French. The interface can be switched via a language switcher. Additional languages can be contributed through the open-source project.

No — Kivvi can be used anywhere. Some features are however Swiss-specific: QR invoices following the Swiss standard, VAT rates (8.1%, 2.6%, 0%), Rappen rounding to 0.05 CHF, and donation receipts under Swiss law. Businesses in Germany or Austria can use Kivvi but need to adapt these compliance fields accordingly.

questions.q: What's the difference from Bexio or Abacus?
questions.a: Bexio and Abacus are general Swiss accounting and ERP software for businesses selling new goods. They can manage stock quantities, invoices, and VAT — but they have no concept of per-item condition grading, donation receipts, per-device repair logs, or impact dashboards. For a secondhand business you end up with workarounds and Excel sheets next to the system. Kivvi solves these problems natively.

Yes — that was a core goal during development. Kivvi offers full goods management with quotes, orders, delivery notes, invoices, and accounting, like Kivitendo. On top, Kivvi brings per-item tracking, condition grading, repair logs, and an impact dashboard — things Kivitendo never properly modelled for secondhand businesses. Data can be exported via CSV from Kivitendo and imported into Kivvi.

questions.q: What's the difference from a normal stock management system?
questions.a: Normal stock systems think in SKUs: "50 Lenovo ThinkPad T14 — quantity: 50". Kivvi thinks in individuals: laptop #23 has scratches on the case, battery 78%, was repaired for CHF 40, suggested price CHF 95, minimum price CHF 70. This difference is fundamental — it enables real per-device margin calculation, quality records, and repair histories that standard stock systems structurally cannot represent.

questions.q: Why not a standard ERP with customisations?
questions.a: Standard ERPs are based on assumptions that are wrong for circular businesses: goods come from suppliers (not donors), have a fixed value at intake (not an assessed one), are tracked as quantities (not individuals), and impact is not a business concept. These assumptions are deeply embedded in the data model. Workarounds cost more time than a system that thinks correctly from day one.

questions.q: Is Kivvi a full ERP or just stock management?
questions.a: Kivvi is a full ERP: contact management (customers, vendors, donors), goods management (intake, stock, sales), document management (quotes, orders, delivery notes, invoices, credit notes), accounting (Swiss SME chart of accounts, journal entries, VAT report), bank reconciliation, and impact dashboard. It covers the full operational cycle.

questions.q: What does Kivvi mean by circular economy?
questions.a: The circular economy includes all businesses that return goods to the economic cycle after their first use: through repair, resale, redesign (upcycling), or parts harvesting. The opposite is the linear economy: make → buy → throw away. Circular businesses interrupt that loop and extend the lifespan of goods.

questions.q: How does Kivvi track individual items?
questions.a: Every item gets a unique ID and a QR code at intake. Attached to it: condition grade (Good/Fair/Poor/For Parts/Scrap), serial number, location, all repair entries with date/cost/hours/note, suggested price, minimum price, intake source (donation/purchase/trade-in/consignment), and finally sale date and price. The full lifecycle is queryable at any time.

Good: barely any signs of use, fully functional. Fair: visible signs of use, works flawlessly. Poor: clear wear, works. For parts: partly broken, suitable as a parts source. Scrap: not repairable, recycling. The grades apply to IT, clothing, furniture, bikes, and other categories with adapted criteria. The condition grade directly influences the suggested price.

questions.q: How does Kivvi calculate impact (CO₂, devices)?
questions.a: The impact dashboard calculates three core metrics: number of items in new use (devices saved), CO₂ savings in kg (count × category-specific factor, e.g. laptop ~300 kg, jeans ~8 kg) and number of people served (transactions). The CO₂ factors are based on lifecycle assessments (Fraunhofer, Ecoinvent). Results can be exported for grant applications.

questions.q: What are donation receipts and how does Kivvi generate them?
questions.a: When someone donates goods (instead of selling them), the donor can deduct that contribution from their tax return — provided your business is recognised as a non-profit. For that they need a donation receipt with mandatory information (name/address of organisation and donor, date, type and value of contribution, confirmation of non-profit status). Kivvi generates this receipt automatically as a PDF at intake — pre-filled and ready to print.

Yes. As soon as a data wipe is recorded for a device — whether through the QC checklist or manually — a PDF certificate can be downloaded. It contains device data (item number, serial number, description), the wipe method (ATA Secure Erase, DBAN, factory reset, etc.), date and operator, plus references to NIST SP 800-88, DIN 66399, and the Swiss FADP. Corporate customers often demand this proof as a precondition for buying back devices.

Yes. In a consignment model, private people drop off goods — the business sells them and keeps a commission. Kivvi records the depositor as a contact, links the items, and enables settlement after sale: what was sold? What's still in stock? What do we still owe? Fully without manual Excel sheets.

Initial setup takes about 10 minutes: company name, address, VAT number, default VAT rate, bank IBAN. Kivvi then automatically creates the Swiss SME chart of accounts (227 accounts), 11 number sequences (invoices, quotes, etc.), and the default warehouse. You can start right away. A full migration from Kivitendo with historical data takes 1–4 hours depending on data volume.

questions.q: Can I import data from Excel?
questions.a: Yes. Kivvi imports CSV files for contacts (customers, vendors), products, and documents (invoices, quotes). Kivvi auto-detects the column structure and proposes a mapping. Swiss number formats (5'007.20) and date formats (22.01.2026) are converted automatically.

questions.q: Can I import data from Kivitendo?
questions.a: Yes — this is explicitly supported. Kivitendo CSV exports are auto-detected. The import order (contacts → products → documents → bookings → stock levels) is enforced and documented by Kivvi. Number sequences are automatically set to the maximum imported number after the import.

questions.q: Does Kivvi work with volunteer teams?
questions.a: Yes. Kivvi is designed so that new staff and volunteers can be onboarded in 5 minutes. The most common actions (intake via AI quick entry, scanning QRs, grading condition, selling items) are reduced to a few clicks. More complex features (accounting, reports) are intended for experienced users.

Kivvi is open source — primary support runs through GitHub Issues and the community. For businesses that deploy Kivvi, we offer direct email support. Reach us at info@revamp-it.ch. For complex setups or migrations we can offer dedicated support.

questions.q: Can I manage multiple sites or warehouses?
questions.a: Yes. Kivvi supports multiple warehouses per business. Items can be transferred between warehouses, stock levels are tracked per location. Multi-tenancy (multiple legally independent businesses in one instance) is also supported.

questions.q: Does Kivvi create Swiss QR invoices?
questions.a: Yes. Every invoice in Kivvi automatically generates a valid Swiss QR payment slip — legally required since 2022. The QR reference is generated automatically, IBAN and recipient data come from the company configuration. The payment slip is included in the invoice PDF and can be used for automatic payment matching (CAMT import).

questions.q: How does Kivvi calculate VAT correctly?
questions.a: Kivvi uses Decimal.js for all financial calculations — no floating-point arithmetic, no rounding errors. VAT is calculated per invoice line (Swiss standard), not on the total. CHF amounts are rounded to 0.05 Rappen (Rappen rounding). VAT rates (8.1%, 2.6%, 0%) come from system configuration, not from code.

Kivvi stores data in a PostgreSQL database. With self-hosting, responsibility for backup, encryption, and access control lies with you. For hosted instances: data is stored in Switzerland, transmission is TLS-encrypted, passwords are hashed (never stored in clear text), each company only sees its own data (multi-tenant isolation at the database level).
With self-hosting: on your own server — you have full control. For hosted instances: in Switzerland, in Swiss data centres. There is no data sale, no analytics passed to third parties.

Kivvi is a web app that runs in the browser — on mobile, tablet, and desktop. There is no native iOS or Android app. The web app works well on mobile for common actions (scanning QR via camera, recording items, changing status). Complex accounting functions are more comfortable on larger screens.

Kivvi imports CAMT.053 files (the Swiss standard for account statements, available at all Swiss banks). Imported transactions are automatically matched against open invoices — via QR reference or amount+date. Transactions not matched automatically are assigned manually.

Yes. Kivvi offers a REST API for contacts, products, and documents. The API is secured with API keys (bearer tokens). It enables integration with external systems — webshops, point-of-sale terminals, barcode-scanner software. API documentation is available in the system under Settings → API.

hero.label: The argument
hero.title: Why a dedicated ERP?
hero.description: Kivvi isn't a universal ERP. It's the operating system for circular businesses — built on different first principles. Eight dimensions that explain why standard ERPs structurally fail.

coreArgument.title: This isn't a feature problem — it's a model problem.
coreArgument.paragraph1: You can use a standard ERP for circular businesses with workarounds. You can build hacks, repurpose custom fields, bend processes. That costs time, nerves, and produces errors.
coreArgument.paragraph2: The real problem runs deeper: standard ERPs were built for a world where goods have a fixed value, come from suppliers, sit in stock, and are sold to customers. Circular businesses work differently — not in some detail, but in their fundamental structure.

dimensions.title: Item tracking
dimensions.erpAssumption: Stock consists of SKUs and quantities. "100 ThinkPad T14" is fully described by product number and unit count.
dimensions.circularReality: Every item is an individual. Laptop #47 has a different battery, different scratches, and a different repair history than laptop #48 — even though both are "ThinkPad T14".
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Every item gets a unique ID, QR code, condition grade, serial number, and full cost history. No SKU thinking.

dimensions.title: Valuation
dimensions.erpAssumption: Value comes from purchase price. All like-for-like items have the same book value. Prices are rule-based (purchase × factor).
dimensions.circularReality: Value is determined by grading. Two identical laptops of the same brand can be CHF 40 apart because one was re-equipped and the other has a display fault.
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Five-grade condition system (good → scrap), combined with suggested price and minimum price per item. Grading determines price — not the other way around.

dimensions.title: Cost accumulation
dimensions.erpAssumption: Costs are known and fixed at intake. Cost basis = purchase price.
dimensions.circularReality: Costs accrue over time: intake price (or CHF 0 for a donation) + cleaning + repair 1 + spare parts + repair 2 = effective cost basis is only known shortly before sale.
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Repair log accumulates all costs per item with date, CHF amount, and hours. Margin is calculated against the current cost basis — always live.

dimensions.title: Source of goods
dimensions.erpAssumption: Goods come from suppliers with an invoice. One source, one accounting transaction.
dimensions.circularReality: Four fundamentally different sources with different legal consequences: donation (→ receipt obligation), purchase (→ supplier invoice), trade-in/return (→ credit note), consignment (→ revenue split after sale).
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Intake recognises all four source types. Donation receipt, supplier document, and consignment log are automatically attached to the transaction.

dimensions.title: Pricing
dimensions.erpAssumption: Prices are rule-based and uniform. Systems optimise for margin targets at the product level.
dimensions.circularReality: Prices are case-by-case: condition of the item, current demand, social discount for the needy, special promo, budget adjustment in the sales conversation. No algorithm can fully automate this.
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Suggested price and minimum price as guardrails. Sales staff can adjust during the conversation. Every price change is logged. The system supports human decisions — it doesn't replace them.

dimensions.title: Donor management
dimensions.erpAssumption: There are suppliers and customers. Both receive documents. Donation logic doesn't exist.
dimensions.circularReality: Donors are neither suppliers nor customers. They get receipts instead of invoices, are handled under Swiss donation law, and the relationship is more valuable to the business long-term than a single purchase.
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Donors are kept as their own contact type. Receipts are generated automatically. Donation history and issued documents are queryable at any time.

dimensions.title: Impact measurement
dimensions.erpAssumption: An ERP tracks money. Impact isn't an ERP topic.
dimensions.circularReality: For circular businesses, impact is a core KPI: how many devices saved? How much CO₂ avoided? How many people supplied with affordable goods? Those numbers decide grants and credibility.
dimensions.kivviAnswer: Impact dashboard computes CO₂ savings, device counts, and people-served from defined values per category. Exportable for grant applications and annual reports.

dimensions.title: Compliance
dimensions.erpAssumption: Standard VAT, standard invoice, standard documents. The legal framework is universal.
dimensions.circularReality: Circular businesses in Switzerland have specific obligations: donation law (receipt content), QR invoice (legally required since 2022), VAT special rules for used goods, data-erasure certificates for IT.
dimensions.kivviAnswer: QR invoices automatic, Rappen rounding (0.05 CHF) correct, donation receipts pre-filled per Swiss law, data-erasure certificates (Swiss FADP / NIST SP 800-88) downloadable. No manual compliance work.

summary.title: The alternative: nothing, or Excel
summary.paragraph1: Many circular businesses today work with Excel sheets, notebooks, or no software at all — not because they don't want a digital solution, but because no available solution fits their operations.
summary.paragraph2: That has consequences: margins are guesses. Impact can't be proven. Donation receipts are typed by hand. Every migration to a new system means data loss.
summary.conclusion: Kivvi isn't a perfect solution — but it's the first that starts with the right model.

hero.title: The circular economy
hero.description: Who are the businesses giving goods a second life? What business models exist? And why do they need different software than everyone else?

definition.title: What is the circular economy?
definition.paragraph1: The linear economy follows a simple pattern: make → buy → throw away. The circular economy breaks that pattern. Goods are repaired, refurbished, resold, transformed, or shared — instead of ending up in landfill.
definition.paragraph2: In Switzerland there are hundreds of businesses that practice this every day: thrift stores, IT refurbishers, repair cafés, clothing exchanges, bike shops. Many are social enterprises. Many work with volunteers. Almost all struggle with the same challenge: their software was never built for them.

participantsSection.title: Who's involved?
participantsSection.intro: The circular economy is broader than people think. Here are the main players:

participants.name: IT refurbishers
participants.description: Collect retired electronics from companies, test, repair, and resell them. Often with data-erasure certificates and corporate customers.

participants.name: Thrift stores & social department stores
participants.description: Accept donated goods and resell them affordably — often with a social mission (integration, employment, affordable supply for low-income households).
participants.examples: Furniture, household goods, clothing, books, toys

participants.name: Repair cafés & workshops
participants.description: Repair broken items — often with volunteers, sometimes professionally. Goal: anchor repair instead of replacement.

participants.name: Vintage & second-hand shops
participants.description: Specialised in specific resaleable categories. Quality and curation are the product.
participants.examples: Clothing, jewellery, watches, furniture, vinyl, collectibles

participants.name: Bike refurbishers
participants.description: Accept old or broken bikes, repair and restore them. A growing market driven by the e-bike boom and urban mobility.
participants.examples: City bikes, e-bikes, road bikes, kids' bikes

participants.name: Upcycling ateliers
participants.description: Process materials and objects into new products. The transformation is part of the value — design as craft.
participants.examples: Pallet furniture, textile upcycling, art objects from waste

participants.name: Social enterprises & NGOs
participants.description: Use circular processes as an employment model or funding source for the social mission. Donation receipts and impact evidence are essential.

participants.name: Take-back programmes
participants.description: Manufacturers or retailers take products back at end-of-life — for refurbishing, redistribution, or recycling.
participants.examples: Electronics manufacturers, fashion chains, furniture retailers

businessModelsSection.title: The business models
businessModelsSection.intro: Not all circular businesses work the same way. Differences in business model determine which software requirements arise.

businessModels.name: Donation → preparation → sale
businessModels.description: The classic thrift-store model. Goods come in for free (donation), are prepared, and sold at social rates. Challenge: costs arise solely from preparation.
businessModels.accounting: Zero purchase price, repair/cleaning costs as cost basis

businessModels.name: Purchase → refurbishing → resale
businessModels.who: IT refurbishers, vintage shops, bike workshops
businessModels.description: Goods are bought cheaply (from companies, auctions, individuals), upgraded, and resold at margin. IT refurbishers and vintage shops.
businessModels.accounting: Purchase price + repair costs = cost basis. Per-unit margin is critical.

businessModels.name: Repair-as-a-service
businessModels.who: Repair cafés (workshop side), bike shops, electricians
businessModels.description: The customer brings a broken device — the business repairs it for a fee. Ownership stays with the customer. Per-job costing is central.
businessModels.accounting: Working hours + spare parts = invoice amount

businessModels.name: Consignment
businessModels.who: Clothing exchanges, second-hand shops, auction houses
businessModels.description: Private people drop off items — the business sells them and keeps a commission. Ownership stays with the depositor until sale.
businessModels.accounting: No purchase, revenue split after sale. Depositor tracking required.

businessModels.name: Upcycling & transformation
businessModels.who: Upcycling ateliers, design studios, social workshops
businessModels.description: Materials are transformed into new products. Value comes from design and craft — not resale of the original.
businessModels.accounting: Materials + work time = cost basis. Product calculation like a craft.

businessModels.name: Parts harvesting
businessModels.description: Broken devices are not repaired but disassembled into parts. Parts are sold separately or used for other repairs.
businessModels.accounting: One device → many parts each with their own value. BOM logic.

businessModels.name: Sharing & exchange
businessModels.who: Libraries of things, tool lending, swap events
businessModels.description: Goods are not sold but lent or exchanged. Membership or usage fees fund the operation.
businessModels.accounting: Fee model, no classic goods sale

dimensionsSection.title: What makes the circular economy fundamentally different
dimensionsSection.intro: These six dimensions explain why standard ERPs structurally fail — and why a dedicated solution is necessary.

dimensions.title: Goods value
dimensions.linear: Defined by purchase price + margin. Identical for all like-for-like goods.
dimensions.circular: Condition-dependent: two identical laptops of the same brand can be CHF 40 apart because one has scratches and the other doesn't.

dimensions.title: Item tracking
dimensions.linear: "100 ThinkPad T14 in stock". SKU + quantity is enough.
dimensions.circular: Every device is an individual with its own ID, condition, history, repair costs, and sale price.

dimensions.title: Costs
dimensions.linear: Known at intake. Fixed. Cost basis = purchase price.
dimensions.circular: Accumulate over time: intake price (or 0 for a donation) + repair 1 + repair 2 + … = cost basis.

dimensions.title: Source of goods
dimensions.linear: Supplier with invoice. One source, one process.
dimensions.circular: Donation (→ receipt), purchase (→ supplier invoice), trade-in (→ credit note), consignment (→ revenue split) — four completely different accounting transactions.

dimensions.title: Pricing
dimensions.linear: Rule-based: purchase price × factor = sale price. Uniform and scalable.
dimensions.circular: Case-by-case decision: condition × demand × social factor. Two identical items, two different prices.

dimensions.title: Impact
dimensions.linear: Not relevant. Software tracks money, not impact.
dimensions.circular: Core KPI: how many devices saved? How much CO₂ avoided? Essential for grant applications, annual reports, and customer communication.

hero.title: The operating system for the global circular economy.
hero.description: Kivvi is the open-source ERP for businesses that give goods a second, third, or fourth life — and our contribution to a world where linear consumption is the exception, not the rule.

mission.title: What we believe
mission.paragraph1: The circular economy isn't a niche. It's the antidote to an economic system that assumes goods are used only once. Thrift stores, IT refurbishers, repair cafés, and vintage shops show every day that the opposite is possible.
mission.paragraph2: The problem: the software these businesses have to use was built for the opposite. For new goods, fixed prices, clean supply chains. No field for condition. No concept of donation receipts. No margin per individual item.
mission.conclusion: Kivvi closes that gap — with an ERP that natively represents the reality of the circular economy, instead of working against it. Our ambition: to become the operating system for circular businesses worldwide.

values.title: What drives Kivvi
values.value1Text: Every product decision asks: does this help businesses giving things a second life? If not, it doesn't belong in here.
values.value2Text: Kivvi is MIT-licensed. Not because there are no alternatives — but because we believe open infrastructure moves the circular economy forward faster than proprietary point solutions.
values.value3Text: Kivvi wasn't born in a product department. It was developed inside a running business — with real processes, real mistakes, real requirements.

openSource.title: Why open source?
openSource.paragraph1: The circular economy is a societal task. When hundreds of thrift stores, repair cafés, and IT refurbishers have the same problems, they should be able to share the same solution — and improve it together.
openSource.paragraph2: Kivvi under the MIT license means: no vendor lock-in, no license fees, no dependence on a single provider. Whoever wants to self-host Kivvi can. Whoever wants to contribute is welcome.
openSource.paragraph3: We believe the best ERP solutions for specific sectors are built by the people working in those sectors — not by software companies that discovered the circular economy as a target market.

team.title: Who builds Kivvi?
team.paragraph1: Kivvi is built by a team that has worked in the circular economy for years — in practice, not just in theory. The requirements don't come from market analyses but from real operations: broken laptops, donation bins, workshop logs, quarterly numbers.
team.paragraph2: That's what makes Kivvi different: when a new feature is built, we know why it's needed — because we had the problem ourselves.
team.paragraph3: Community contributors are welcome. If you work in a circular business and have ideas to make Kivvi better — we listen.

comparison.title: The circular economy's software problem
comparison.intro: No existing ERP connects all the parts — each fails for structural reasons. Kivvi was built because the gap was too big and too costly to close with workarounds.

competitors.name: Bexio
competitors.verdict: 100,000+ Swiss SMEs, QR invoices, CAMT — accounting-solid. Fails on the foundational assumption: stock is quantity, not individuals. No donations, no condition, no impact. The March 2026 price hike is pushing customers to evaluate.

competitors.name: Odoo
competitors.verdict: Open source, extensible, Odoo 19 with serious AI. But: CHF 5,000–30,000 for a Swiss base setup, then circular workflows from scratch. A motivated partner could build it — would take years.

competitors.name: Abacus
competitors.verdict: The Swiss accounting standard for mid-sized companies. Implementations from CHF 20,000. No circular-specific functionality — and no incentive to build it for 20-person non-profits.

competitors.name: Kivitendo ★
competitors.verdict: Inspired Kivvi. Mature Perl codebase, QR invoices, SME chart of accounts. No per-item tracking, no condition grading, no impact dashboard, no modern UI. Kivvi imports Kivitendo data directly via CSV.

competitors.name: RepairShopr / RepairDesk
competitors.verdict: Mature repair tickets, customer messaging, parts tracking. Not a full ERP: no double-entry accounting, no QR invoices, no balance sheet. Accounting has to be solved separately.

competitors.name: Kivvi
competitors.verdict: Connects all the parts: Swiss compliance, intake, condition grading, repair workflow, accounting, QR invoices, donation receipts, and impact reporting — natively for the circular economy.

pipeline.desc: Reuse rate, CO₂ avoided (by category), items rescued from the linear cycle. Configurable CO₂ factors per product category.

pipeline.title: Multi-tenant & self-hosting

pipeline.title: Repair workflow
pipeline.desc: Repair orders with technician assignment, hours, and status tracking. Repair queue, parts tracking (per-part cost capture), log, and AI commands (cost/hours, condition, status, data wipe, QC checklist).

pipeline.title: Webshop integration

datenschutz.title: Privacy policy
datenschutz.validity: Effective from 1 January 2025 · In accordance with the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP)

section2.title: 2. What data we collect
section2.accountText: On registration we collect email address, company name, and a password (stored as a hash).
section2.usageText: The application stores the business data you enter (contacts, products, documents) — solely to provide the service.
section2.logsText: Server-side logs (IP address, timestamps, requested URLs) are kept for a maximum of 30 days and used solely for fault diagnosis.

section3.title: 3. Purpose of data processing
purposes: Provision and operation of the Kivvi application
section3.noAdvertising: We do not use your data for advertising and do not share it with third parties.

section4.title: 4. Storage location and hosting
section4.text: All data is stored on servers in Switzerland or the EU. For self-hosted installations, the choice of storage location lies with the operator of that instance.

section5.title: 5. Retention period
section5.text: Account data is retained for as long as the account is active. After account deletion, personal data is removed within 30 days, unless statutory retention obligations apply (e.g. Swiss accounting obligation under OR 958f: 10 years).

section6.title: 6. Your rights
section6.intro: Under the FADP you have the right to:
rights: Information about the data stored about you
section6.exercise: To exercise these rights please contact:

section7.title: 7. Cookies
section7.text: Kivvi uses functional cookies only for authentication (session cookie). No tracking cookies, analytics cookies, or advertising cookies are used.

section8.title: 8. Changes to this policy
section8.text: We reserve the right to adjust this privacy policy as needed. The current version is always available on this page. Registered users will be informed by email of substantial changes.
